prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: Checkout A/B Test Results (language en).
Grid: 7 columns × 9 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "Metric" spans 1 col × 2 row; "Control" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Variant" spans 2 col × 1 row; "Lift" spans 1 col × 2 row; "p-value" spans 1 col × 2 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Metric" · longest unbreakable word 100px · one-line width 263px
  col 2: header "Control › Mean" · longest unbreakable word 50px · one-line width 52px
  col 3: header "Control › 95% CI" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 113px
  col 4: header "Variant › Mean" · longest unbreakable word 49px · one-line width 50px
  col 5: header "Variant › 95% CI" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 110px
  col 6: header "Lift" · longest unbreakable word 52px · one-line width 52px
  col 7: header "p-value" · longest unbreakable word 47px · one-line width 55px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"poor","why":"The confidence intervals have ample room, but the narrow metric column breaks words and stretches labels across three or four lines, making rows difficult to scan."},"B":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Metric labels remain readable and the two test groups are balanced, but the currency and time confidence intervals split across lines, making comparisons harder."},"C":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Both groups have balanced proportions, all numeric values and intervals stay on one line, and metric labels wrap naturally without breaking words."},"D":{"grade":"bad","why":"Nearly equal column widths waste space on short values while breaking a metric word and splitting several confidence intervals; the tall rows are hard to scan."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"The wider metric column keeps most labels compact and the groups balanced, though currency and time confidence intervals wrap across lines."},"F":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Metric labels are compact, but the p-value header, time means, and several confidence intervals wrap, disrupting the comparison of results."}},"best":["C"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"B and E make a reasonable tradeoff for wider metric labels, but the split confidence intervals make them less effective for comparing results."}
